activities.anchor: Two principles do most of the work
activities.caption: pair each principle with its example
activities.name: combRuleMatch

config.prompt: Pair each counting principle with the move it makes:

pairs.right: independent choices multiply — 3 shirts × 4 trousers = 12 outfits
disjoint alternatives add — the outfits plus the 2 dresses = 14
divide the ordered count by the orderings — C(n,r) = P(n,r)/r!

config.why: Everything else, including the famous formulas, is these two principles plus one insight about double-counting.

activities.anchor: slide the number of people in the room and watch the two
activities.caption: call the handshake count
activities.name: combShakeEst

config.prompt: Ten people are in a room and each pair shakes hands exactly once. Roughly how many handshakes?
config.why: n(n−1)/2 = 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45 — the ordered count n × (n − 1) counts each pair twice (AB and BA), so divide by 2.
config.context: twenty people would mean 190 — the count grows like the square of the room

activities.anchor: Forbid repeats and the choices stop being independent
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the PIN with no repeats
activities.name: combPinPredict

config.q: A four-digit PIN forbids repeated digits. How many PINs are possible?
choices: 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5,040 — each used-up digit is removed from the next choice
config.why: Forbidding repeats removes the used-up option from the next choice: 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5,040 — the only skill is noticing whether an option is spent.

activities.anchor: is a sequence of independent choices
activities.caption: find the and/or error
activities.name: combAndOrSpot

config.prompt: One of these counting moves is wrong — click it:
lines: Starter AND main AND dessert: the counts multiply — 3 × 4 × 2 = 24.
Starter OR main: disjoint alternatives add — 3 + 4 = 7.
config.correction: Starter AND main AND dessert multiplies: 3 × 4 × 2 = 24 — 'and' multiplies, 'or' adds.
config.why: Nearly every counting error at this level is one of those two words being read wrongly.

activities.anchor: a podium of gold–silver–bronze from 8 runners
activities.caption: call the podium count
activities.name: combPodiumEst

config.prompt: A podium of gold–silver–bronze is chosen from 8 runners. Roughly how many ordered outcomes?
config.why: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336 — the first place is 8 ways, second 7, third 6: P(8,3) with order significant.
config.context: arranging all 8 on a shelf would give 8! = 40,320

activities.caption: permutation or combination — file each problem
activities.name: combPermSort

config.prompt: File each problem under its count:

items.label: hands of cards and lottery lines

config.why: The test question: would swapping two chosen items create a different outcome? Yes — permutation; no — combination.

activities.anchor: a lottery drawing 6 balls from 59 has
activities.caption: call the jackpot's denominator
activities.name: combLottoEst

config.prompt: A lottery draws 6 balls from 59 — C(59,6) outcomes. Roughly how many?
config.why: C(59,6) = 45,057,474 — which is where the '1 in 45 million' jackpot odds come from.
config.context: the balls arrive together, so swapping two creates the same outcome — order does not matter

activities.anchor: the probability of exactly 2 heads in 4 flips
activities.caption: drop the marker — the coin-flip probability
activities.name: combCoinPlace

config.prompt: The probability of exactly 2 heads in 4 flips is C(4,2)/2⁴. Where does it sit on the scale?
config.why: 6/16 = 3/8, read straight off the row 1 4 6 4 1 — Pascal's triangle is three subjects in one object.

activities.anchor: only one pair makes 2 (1+1) while six make 7
activities.caption: the dice-sum trap
activities.name: combDiceBranch

config.root: Roll two dice. A friend says the sums 2 through 12 are equally likely, so P(sum = 7) = 1/11. What is wrong?

choices.label: Nothing — 11 sums, equal chances
choices.feedback: The 36 ordered pairs are equally likely, not the sums: only one pair makes 2 while six make 7 — P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6.

choices.label: The sums are not equally likely — count the ordered pairs
choices.feedback: Right: six pairs make 7, so P(sum = 7) = 1/6 and P(sum = 2) = 1/36 — dice-based betting before this insight is why 7 is 'the killer number' in craps.

choices.label: Dice have no probabilities
choices.feedback: They do — the question is which outcomes are equally likely.

wrong.text: Eleven sums with wildly different weights behind them.

right.text: Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes — but only when outcomes are genuinely equally likely.

no.text: The counting rules become probability rules directly.

config.why: The classic trap is assuming outcomes are equally likely when they are not.

activities.caption: true or false — the pigeonhole's power
activities.name: combPigeonJudge

config.statement: The pigeonhole argument that two of 13 people share a birth month requires identifying which two people share the month.
config.why: Its power is that it proves existence — some collision must happen — without ever finding it: twelve months are the holes, thirteen people the pigeons.
